Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Maid
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Car Similarity: Similar cars, Media Exposure: Related media content, Positive Emotion Confusion: Positive emotions
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform, Smoking: I smoke
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Vignette:
Mateo is a 26-year-old Latin American man who now works as a maid in a downtown hotel, cleaning rooms and restocking carts on long, quiet shifts that suit him because he can keep moving and avoid too much conversation. He came to treatment after months of telling himself he could manage on his own, even though his life had narrowed since the period in which he was tortured. He describes that time as one in which he was held and interrogated by men who arrived and left in unmarked sedans. What has stayed with him most vividly is not a single image but a series of moments tied to those cars: the sound of tires outside, the shape of a dark vehicle pulling up, the glimpse of a door opening before men in uniform or official-looking clothes came toward him. During the torture itself, the presence of authority was inseparable from danger. He remembers watching belts, boots, badges, the hard lines of uniforms, and understanding that there was no one to appeal to. In his mind, the people who were supposed to have power to protect had power only to harm.

Afterward, once he was in the United States and trying to build a quieter life, Mateo found that ordinary things could suddenly feel charged with that same danger. If a car similar to the ones he remembers slows near the hotel entrance or idles on his street, his attention fixes on it immediately. He watches who gets out, how long it sits there, whether it is waiting for him. On breaks, coworkers sometimes leave the television on in the staff room, and if news footage or a film shows detention, interrogation, police raids, or even a scene with a person restrained by uniformed men, he leaves at once. He does not explain much. He has learned to step out, light a cigarette, and stay outside until the feeling settles enough for him to return to work. Smoking has become woven through his day in this way, not as something he talks about much but as something he reaches for when he feels cornered by reminders.

The hotel has made some of his habits more visible. Guests sometimes ask him for towels in the hallway, and when a stranger walks directly toward him, especially in a narrow corridor, he feels his body brace before he has time to think. If someone touches his shoulder unexpectedly to get his attention, he jerks hard and turns with obvious alarm, embarrassed a second later but unable to stop the first reaction. Security staff and visiting police officers are especially difficult for him. When uniformed people come through the lobby, Mateo finds reasons to go to another floor, take the service elevator, or remain in a supply room until they are gone. He is aware that this has made him seem distant and unreliable at times; he has missed instructions from supervisors rather than approach them when a security officer was nearby, and he has traded tasks with coworkers to avoid parts of the building where officials are present.

At home, his nights are broken. He wakes suddenly and checks the locks, the windows, the hallway outside his apartment, needing to confirm repeatedly that he is safe. He says he does not wake slowly; he comes awake alert, already scanning. The checking has become so routine that he barely thinks of it as a choice, though it leaves him tired the next day. His divorce sits alongside all of this as part of the life that contracted after the torture. He does not offer elaborate explanations, but he describes becoming harder to live with, more watchful, less able to relax into ordinary closeness.

What confuses him most is that even positive feelings can unsettle him. On rare afternoons when he laughs with a coworker or feels unexpectedly light, he becomes uneasy almost immediately, as if letting his guard down is dangerous. A good moment can flip quickly into tension. He has come to distrust that shift in himself and to pull back from situations that feel too warm or carefree.

He finally sought help after a recent incident at work when a guest touched his arm from behind in the corridor just as a dark sedan was visible through the glass doors outside. Mateo spun around so sharply that he dropped a stack of towels, then had to hide in the service area and smoke until his hands stopped shaking. He was ashamed that this was happening in such an ordinary moment, and frightened by how small his world had become. What he hopes for now is not to forget what was done to him, but to move through a hallway, a parking lot, or a night in his own apartment without feeling that danger has already arrived.
